job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Hassan Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now, in your job hunt, your first job or your studies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior backend developer at a payments company in Middlesbrough that builds software for small shops to take card payments. I started three months ago. I write and test small pieces of code that move payment data around, and I'm on call one week in six, which pays a bit extra. I studied computer science, passed with an average mark and no internship. I use AI tools all day, to write code, find bugs and explain things I don't know. In the evenings and on Saturdays I help my dad in his grocery shop, and I build websites for local shops, mostly for cash. I rent a room in a shared house, and Friday prayers and family dinners matter to me a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because most people are already using it and the world hasn't ended. At work I'd tell my lead, Priyanka, that the tools help a lot with routine code, and that's all. To family I'd say nothing's changed, so don't worry. Online I'd say let the market decide what works, which it always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changes, which means the loan stays big and my savings stay tiny. I earn a low wage, I've got under a month's money saved and I give my mum a little for the house. The payments company is growing but it's young and could be bought, which worries me more than AI. And there aren't many other tech jobs around Middlesbrough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and doing the websites on the side. I'd try to get the shop sites up to six or seven clients, because every one is about £300. I'd save £100 a month. And I'd keep helping my dad, because that's what family does, and because it's cheaper than hiring someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine. I'd say focused, not afraid. I'm tense about money but I always have been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you get the website clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's shop was the first. A customer asked who made the site, then asked if I'd do one for his barbershop. It spread by word of mouth, mostly in the mosque and the market. I don't advertise. It works because people trust me, and I'd rather get a customer through a friend than through a stranger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company could be bought. What happens to you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: New owners usually cut the people who don't have a clear value. I'm three months in, and I'd be one of those. I'd want the sites to bring in enough to buy me three months of breathing space. That's why I'm pushing them so hard.

I'd say let the **market** decide what works.
think: Nothing changes, so the **loan** stays big and my savings tiny.
The payments company is young and could be **bought**, which worries me more than AI.
do: Build up the shop **websites** to six or seven clients at about £300 each.
Keep helping my **dad** in the grocery shop.
feel: Focused, not afraid, but tense about **money** as I always am.

steps.text: Sign six more local shops for websites at £300 each
Save £100 a month from pay and website fees

Use the AI coding assistant to finish routine code faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest change since the internet, and the people who use it will do better. At work I'd tell Priyanka we should automate our testing and our support first, before a competitor does it to us. To family I'd say a small business can use these tools to compete with bigger ones. Online I'd say governments should stay out of the way, but make sure schools teach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it helps me and hurts me. I'm fast with the tools, so I'm worth more than a graduate who isn't. But the company needs fewer developers for the same work, and I'm the cheapest, so I'm either the one they keep or the one they don't need. I'd say it's fifty-fifty. I'd like to be the one who builds the thing that replaces the routine work, not the one it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to build the company's AI testing tool, and tie it to a measurable result like fewer bugs. I'd take on more clients for the websites, using AI to build them in an afternoon. I'd start a small business, offering AI set-up for local shops, with my dad's grocery as the first customer. And I'd cut my own spending to the bone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and a bit sharp. I like being ahead, but I know being ahead isn't the same as being safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would AI set-up for a local shop look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A system that answers customers' messages, tracks stock and writes the weekly order. My dad spends two hours a night on that with a pen. I'd build it for him and charge other shops £50 a month. Fifty shops would be £2,500 a month, which is more than I earn now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want free markets and little government interference. What do you say to people who lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say help them with training and with their families, and let communities do it first. I don't like handouts that go on for ever, but I do think there should be a fair start. I've seen how the mosque and the shop help people through bad patches. That works better than forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast, and people should be honest about it. At work I'd ask Priyanka whether there's a plan. To my family I'd say save, stay close and learn something people will always need. Online I'd say I'd want the market to adjust but I'd also want some breathing space for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think a payments company is exactly where AI gets going first. In two years, it could write the code I write, and test it too. I'd lose my wage in the first year, I think, unless I've turned into the one who runs the machines. My dad's shop sells food, which people need, but it isn't a gold mine, and he's fifty-eight. I'd be scared for the whole family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the side business hard from day one, because it's the only thing that's mine. I'd try to sign twenty local shops in six months. I'd cut my own costs to the bone, and I'd move back into my parents' house to save on rent. I'd also work out whether I could get a hands-on job, like fitting shop systems, which robots can't do for about three years. And I'd lean on the mosque community for contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a race with a deadline I can't move. I'm not frozen, I'm running, but I'm very aware that I could trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty shops in six months is a lot. How would you do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do two a week through the people I already know: barbers, takeaways, phone repair shops. I'd offer the first month free and a simple promise, if it doesn't save you time I don't charge. With AI I can set up one in a day. I'd do it in the evenings, and give up sleep if I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be scared for the whole family. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's shop is open fourteen hours a day and it only just covers the house. If I lose my job, there's no spare money for anybody. My younger sister Layla (his sister) is starting university and she'll borrow too. I'm the one my family thinks has a safe career. I haven't told them it might not be.

I'd tell my family to **save**, stay close and learn something people will always need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start, if you use it. At work I'd tell Priyanka we should aim to be the company that uses AI best, not worst. To my family I'd say it's coming, and we should get ready, not scared. Online I'd say let people build things, and keep the rules simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm cautiously optimistic. I'm good with the tools, I've got a side business, and five years lets me grow it into something real. The fear is that a bigger competitor does the same thing cheaper. But local shops like to deal with someone they know, so I'd have a niche.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the shop services into a proper company with a partner, probably a friend from uni who does design. I'd keep my job for the first two years for the income. I'd save for a deposit and for a small marriage fund. And I'd keep learning, by building one small new thing a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good. I'm a bit proud, a bit nervous. There's a lot of work, but it's work I want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a marriage fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents want me to marry within a few years, and it's a big family event. Weddings cost, and my family couldn't pay for much of mine. I'd rather pay for it myself and not be a burden. I also want to be in a position to support a family, which I couldn't do on my current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to leave the payments job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the business covers my rent and food for six months in a row. Not before. I'd also give Priyanka plenty of notice, because she's been good to me. I'd want to leave on good terms in a town where everyone knows everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and it'll be a good thing for people who build. At work I'd say let's design for 2036 now. To family I'd say stay close and save. Online I'd say the market will sort the winners from the losers, but we should look after people who are slow to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm calm. Ten years is long enough to pay off the loan, build a company and look after my parents. I might even have a shop of my own, selling something real alongside the digital side. What I worry about is whether I'll still be hungry in ten years, when I've got a family and a house. Comfort could be my enemy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the company to about ten staff, mostly local people I train. I'd marry and buy a house near my parents. I'd put some money into my dad's shop, maybe a second branch with a delivery side. And I'd keep studying AI, because I think the field changes every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels bright, and I'm slightly nervous about saying so, as if I'm tempting fate. I'd say calm, with a lot to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to people who lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd hire them and train them if I could. I mean that. I'd also say they shouldn't be ashamed, because it isn't their fault. The best way I know to help is to give someone work, and a company can do that more directly than a government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stay hungry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By setting a new target every year that scares me a bit, and by keeping a few people around me who'll tell me when I'm slacking. My dad is one. He was in the shop at six this morning and he's still there. That's what I'm up against.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I could build a company in five years, but two years gives me no time to get there before my wage goes, and my family can't carry me. What would help is quick access to small business loans, rules that keep things simple, and customers who still want to deal with someone they know.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that people my age aren't afraid of work, we're afraid of being told there isn't any. I'm willing to build something and I'm willing to be up at six. What I want is a fair chance and a few years of breathing space.

headlineQuote: People my age aren't afraid of work, we're afraid of being told there isn't any.
portrait: Hassan is a 22-year-old computer science graduate working as a **junior backend developer** at a payments firm in Middlesbrough.
He is traditional and adaptive: he uses AI all day, builds websites for local shops, and helps in his father's grocery.
His cushion is thin, with heavy debt, under a month saved and a family that cannot help.
He is uneasy when little changes and alarmed at two years because his family thinks his career is safe.
His answer to change is to build a business and hire local people.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because his wage could go before his business is ready and his family can't carry him.
whatWouldHelp: Quick access to **small business** loans, simple rules, and customers who still prefer someone they know.
